The words

Bless, O Lord, each opening year
To the souls assembling here:
Clothe Thy word with power divine,
Make us willing to be Thine.

Where Thou hast Thy work begun,
Give new strength the race to run;
Scatter darkness, doubts, and fears,
Wipe away the mourner's tears.

Bless us all, both old and young;
Call forth praise from every tongue:
Let our whole assembly prove
All Thy power and all Thy love!

How to sing it from the solfa

  • Find doh first. Play or hum F and sing d r m f s up from it, so the whole choir has the key in their ears before you start.
  • Pitch the first note. The tune starts on m (A).
  • Count the time. 4/4 means four crotchet beats in each bar. In the grid every cell is half a crotchet: a dash (–) holds the note before it, and _ is a rest.
  • Know the notes. The tune uses d r m f s l t and the chromatic fe. A comma after a note (s,) is the octave below; an apostrophe (d') is the octave above.

About the hymn

John Newton wrote these words. They were printed in the supplement of the 1866 edition of A Book of Hymns for Public and Private Devotion, compiled by Samuel Longfellow and Samuel Johnson (Boston, 1866), as hymn 566, “New Year”.

The book printed the words without tunes, marked Sevens (7.7.7.7) (7.7.7.7), to be sung to any tune of that metre. This page sets them to HEINLEIN; any other Sevens (7.7.7.7) tune fits them as well.

  • Words: John Newton (1725–1807)
  • Music, attributed (1676): Martin Herbst (died undefined)
  • Music (1676): Nurnberg (died undefined)

Questions about Bless, O Lord, Each Opening Year

What is the doh of Bless, O Lord, Each Opening Year?

In this version, in D minor, doh is F. If your choir sings it in another key, doh moves to the new key note and every solfa syllable stays the same — that is what movable doh means.

What note does Bless, O Lord, Each Opening Year start on?

It starts on m (A in D minor). Find doh first, then sing up or down to m.

Is Bless, O Lord, Each Opening Year in the public domain?

Yes. John Newton died in 1807, Martin Herbst died in undefined, Nurnberg died in undefined; the words were in print by 1866 and the music in 1676. Everyone named died before 1955 and both were published before 1929, so the hymn is out of copyright in the UK, the EU, the United States and Nigeria. Modern arrangements and translations can still be under copyright.
